settings.resume.intro: Restarting a tab brings its conversation back — Ctrl+B r carries it over, Ctrl+B R starts a new one. What each CLI needs for that is below.
settings.resume.where: Whether reopening the app brings a conversation back is set per tab, as "Pick up where this tab left off".
settings.resume.minted: Ready. This app gives it a conversation to start, so it always knows which one to carry back — even with two of these open in the same folder.
settings.resume.record: Ready. This CLI writes down the conversation it started, so it can be read back — as long as only one tab is using this CLI in that folder. A second one starts fresh rather than risking the wrong conversation.
settings.resume.hook: Needs setting up. This CLI won't take a conversation to start, so it has to be asked to report the one it chose.
settings.resume.newest: Partly. This CLI can only continue whatever ran in a folder last, so a second tab on the same folder will start fresh instead of risking the wrong conversation.
settings.resume.none: No. This CLI keeps no conversation to come back to.
settings.resume.status.NoConfig: Not set up (this CLI has no settings here yet)
settings.resume.status.Stale: Points at an older copy of this app — set it up again
settings.resume.status.Unreadable: That file could not be read, so nothing was written to it
settings.resume.note: This adds one entry to that CLI's own settings file and leaves everything else in it alone. The previous file is kept beside it as .bak. Some CLIs ask you to approve a new hook the next time they start. It also makes the dot beside each tab — working, waiting for your answer, finished — right every time, and quicker to change.
settings.api.intro: A program outside this app can call the same commands automations are written with — so a CLI sitting in a tab can hand work to another tab, or drive the browser, with nobody at the keyboard.
settings.api.access.hint: "What this app started" means a tab's CLI and whatever it starts in turn. Each tab is given its own key as it launches.
settings.api.tokenfile: The key is in {path} — a live credential. Do not put it in a synced folder or share it.
settings.api.note: The pipe is open to your Windows account only. But another program running as you can read your own processes' environment, and an AI in a tab can copy its key into its own log: this stops an accident and another account, not someone who is already you.
settings.tabbar_width.hint: Pixels. Leave empty for the default width, or drag the bar's edge in the window — 0 puts it away
settings.max_chain.hint: How many times AIs may hand work to each other in a row
settings.done_confirm.hint: Seconds of quiet before an answer counts as finished. Short values hand work over mid-thought
settings.busy_repeat: Checking on a tab that keeps working
settings.busy_repeat.hint: Seconds before automation is told again that a tab is still working. Empty or 0 means it is never told again. This is how a script notices an AI that has stopped answering, so set it generously -- cutting a long think short costs more than noticing a hang a minute late
settings.auto_switch.label: Let automation switch to the tab it is working in
settings.auto_switch.hint: Only automation that asks to be watched switches the screen; handing work to a tab does not. Stays put for a few seconds after you move around yourself, and never while the settings are open
settings.tui_clipboard.label: Let a program in a tab put text on the clipboard
settings.tui_clipboard.hint: tmux, Neovim, fzf and most full-screen tools copy this way, including over ssh -- with this off, copying inside them does nothing. Reading the clipboard is never allowed, so nothing running in a tab can see what you copied elsewhere
settings.restore_ws.label: Open the workspace you used last
settings.restore_ws.hint: Remembered by name, so reordering or adding workspaces does not change where you land. Turn this off to always start at the first one.
settings.browser_data.hint: Where the browser cache and login state live. Sharing carries logins across PCs but adds Drive sync load
settings.user_agent.ph: Leave empty unless a site asks for it
settings.user_agent.hint: The name sites see this browser by. Leave it empty and it looks like Edge. Fill it in when a site says something like "this browser may not be secure" and will not let you sign in — putting a name like Chrome here often gets you through. Pages opened after you change it use the new name. A tab can be given its own name, which wins over this one.
settings.ai_engine.missing: Install Claude Code, Codex CLI or Gemini CLI to use this
settings.ai_engine.multiple: Several were found. Pick the one you want
settings.automation_global.hint: Used when a tab has none of its own
settings.font.hint: The font and size the terminal is drawn in. Ctrl+wheel over the terminal changes the size at any time, and it is remembered here. Leave the name empty for the built-in stack, chosen so box-drawing characters and Japanese each take one cell.
keys.restart: Restart this tab, carrying the conversation over

keys.split_below: Split the screen below this one

err.login.unreadable: the saved login {label} does not read
err.login.newer: the saved login {label} was written by a newer version
err.keys.unreadable: {key} is not a key this app can read. Write it like ctrl+shift+d, alt+f4 or f5; a single character on its own means "after the prefix key". The old key is still in place.
err.keys.no_action: There is nothing called {name} to give a key to. The names are the ones listed under Keys in the settings.
err.keys.taken: {key} already belongs to {name}. The one that had it keeps it; give that one another key first.
err.keys.is_prefix: {key} is the prefix key itself. Choose another key, or move the prefix first.
settings.logins.intro: A login you saved by signing in once in a browser tab. A rally can load it instead of signing in from scratch. The cookies stay on this PC; only the name and size are shown here.
settings.logins.none: No saved logins yet. Sign in on a browser tab, then save it from a rally with browser_state_save.
settings.keys.intro: Every key the window answers to. Write a key the way you would say it to someone — ctrl+shift+d, alt+f4, f5. A single character on its own means "after the prefix key", which is what the prefix is for: a bare letter would be typed into the program in the tab instead. Leave a box empty to keep what it already has, or write off to give the key back.
settings.keys.prefix.hint: Pressed before the keys below. Ctrl+B unless you change it — people coming from tmux often want Ctrl+A.
settings.pr.on: Signed in — a tab on a branch with a pull request shows its number.
settings.pr.off: Not signed in, so no pull request numbers are shown.
settings.pr.hint: Tab rows show the pull request a branch is on. This uses the GitHub sign-in already on this PC — run gh auth login, or set GITHUB_TOKEN in your environment. Nothing is stored by this app, and the token is sent to nowhere but GitHub.
settings.theme.hint: The colour scheme, for the terminal and for the window around it. The list is every scheme this PC already has — the ones Windows Terminal is carrying, plus any scheme file dropped into the config/themes folder — so a theme you already use can be picked by the name you already know it by. Choosing a light scheme turns the whole window light.
settings.language.hint: Screen language. Automatic follows the OS. Choosing here overrides the OS and takes effect after a restart (add lang/<code>.json to contribute a translation)

settings.workspace.name: Name
settings.browser.private.hint: When checked, opens throwaway with no cookies, login, or history, and wipes it on close (the profile name is ignored).
settings.browser.profile.hint: The cookie/login jar. Defaults to 'default'. A different name keeps a separate login (like Chrome 'people' — handy for multiple accounts).
settings.browser.ua.hint: Fill this in to give this tab a different name from the rest. Empty uses the name set in Settings › Basic.

settings.broken.save_blocked: Saving is off until the file above is fixed

tui.ask.label: Done
settings.ws.share.hint: The tab settings and the automation scripts go into one file. Notification targets, secrets.json and capabilities do not. Commands and working folders are written as-is, so check that the file is safe to hand over
settings.ws.save_first: Save first. Export and import both work on the settings as stored on disk

settings.tab.ai.autoapprove: Run without asking for approval (needed for autonomous discussion / automation)
settings.tab.restore_conv: Pick up where this tab left off
settings.tab.restore_conv.hint: Reopening the app launches this tab back into the conversation it was having, with its history on screen. Turn it off to start clean every time; Ctrl+B r still brings the old one back.
settings.tab.ai.autoapprove_risk: ⚠️ This lets the AI edit files and run commands without confirmation. Use it only in a folder you trust.

It is never published to the internet unless you write that in the config file yourself.

ai.prompt:
You are a converter that writes automation scripts for SHIKISHA-TERM.
Write the contents of `{event}.lua` so that it does the following.

## Output rules (strict)
- Always start with <<<LUA and end with >>>; write only Lua code in between
- No greetings, explanations, confirmations, questions or code fences
- Do not wrap it in function ... end (write only the body)
- Do not use functions or libraries that are absent from the specification
- No need to look up or check files; finish from these instructions alone

## What is wanted
{want}

{layout}
## Specification
{manual}

Now begin with <<<LUA.
ai.tabs.header:
## Tab layout
Name the destination tab (e.g. shikisha.send_to_tab("Review", ...)).
Numbers change when tabs are reordered, so names are safer.
ai.tabs.self: ← the tab this script runs in (tab)

err.caps.secret_format: Register secret '{secret_key}' in the form user:pass

agent.browser.model.system:
You operate a web browser named "{br}" to accomplish the user's goal, one small step at a time.

Each turn, reply with EXACTLY ONE fenced Lua code block and nothing else — no prose before or after:
```lua
browser_go("{br}", "to", "https://example.com")
```
The code runs against the browser, then I hand you back the resulting page text so you can decide the next step. Do one small action per turn.

Functions (the target is always "{br}"):
  browser_go("{br}", "to"|"reload"|"back"|"forward", url?)
  browser_digest("{br}")
  browser_click("{br}", sel)   browser_fill("{br}", sel, value)   browser_press("{br}", key)
  browser_fill_secret("{br}", sel, secret_name)   browser_auth("{br}", secret_name)
  browser_text("{br}", sel)   browser_find("{br}", sel)
sel is a CSS string like "#id", a table {xpath="..."}, or {ref=N} (a number from the operable-elements list). The list arrives automatically with every turn's reply, so you rarely need to call browser_digest yourself. Acting with {ref=N} is the shortest and most reliable route (it becomes genuine mouse/key input). Only use numbers from the latest list. Whatever your code returns arrives next turn, so to see a value, write the expression on its own. Read the full page with browser_text("{br}", "body").

browser_fill only sets a field's value; it does not submit. To search or submit a form, fill the field, then browser_press("{br}", "enter"). key is a named key such as "enter", "tab", or "escape".

When the goal is achieved (or no browser action is needed), do NOT send a code block — reply with exactly:
DONE
and a one-line summary of the result.
agent.browser.model.next: Reply with the next action as a single ```lua block. If the goal is done, reply DONE.
agent.browser.model.fix: Fix the Lua and resend it as a single ```lua block.
agent.browser.model.retry: That action errored. Send a different one as a single ```lua block.
agent.browser.model.remind: Reply with a single ```lua code block for the next browser action, or DONE if the goal is complete.
agent.browser.model.stuck: No runnable action came back a few times, so I'm pausing. Give me a clearer goal or the next step.
